title: Lukewarm (Apocalypse 3:14–22)
tomorrow: I stand at the gate and knock

lines: A COFFEE, NEITHER HOT NOR COLD.
cards: You order a coffee and take a sip. Not hot. You'd have happily taken iced coffee, cold and sharp, or a steaming cup that warms your hands.
But this one has sat under the lamp too long, and it's neither. You set it down and don't pick it up again. Everyone knows the face people make at a lukewarm drink.
The last of the seven letters in the Apocalypse uses that face, and it goes to a city that had money, comfort and, if the historians are right, a water problem.

teach.h: A RICH CITY THAT REBUILT ITSELF.
teach.b: Laodicea was rich, a banking town known for fine wool and for an eye medicine.
The Roman historian Tacitus records that when an earthquake struck it in the year sixty, the city rebuilt from its own wealth, without help from Rome.

Now Christ's words to its church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold, nor hot. I would thou wert cold, or hot. But because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold, nor hot, I will begin to vomit thee out of my mouth."
Strong language: the face at the coffee cup. Many scholars point to the city's water. Nearby Hierapolis had well-known hot springs, good for healing.

Colossae, not far off, had cold, fresh water, good for drinking. Laodicea's water, on this reading, came through a long aqueduct and arrived tepid. Read that way, hot and cold aren't zealous and hostile.
Both are useful: one heals, one refreshes. Lukewarm does neither. And the church's problem matches the city's pride.

teach.h: RICH, BUT POOR, BLIND AND NAKED.
teach.b: Thou sayest, I am rich and have need of nothing, the letter goes on, and knowest not that thou art poor, and blind, and naked. A city of eye medicine, but blind. A city of wool, but naked.
So Christ counsels them to get true gold, white garments and salve for their eyes from him.

teach.h: SUCH AS I LOVE, I REBUKE.
teach.b: Then, so the harshness isn't misread: "Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise." A rebuke from someone who wants them back, not a door slammed. The very next verse is about a door, and who is standing outside it.

how: Catholic spiritual writers have long warned against lukewarmness, or spiritual sloth, and Catholics often fight it with small, regular commitments: a daily prayer time, weekly Mass, a monthly confession, done wholeheartedly.

o: half-hearted: useful neither for healing nor refreshing
cold toward God and openly against the faith
calm and steady, never carried away by feeling

games.q: the letter to Laodicea — tap the pairs.

s: Laodicea was a poor, struggling city
it was rich; Tacitus says it rebuilt from its own wealth after an earthquake.
the letter's harsh words come with a statement of love
such as I love, I rebuke and chastise.
in one common reading, both hot and cold are good things
hot water heals, cold water refreshes. lukewarm does neither.

games.q: your church is comfortable and well-off. a letter arrives: you are neither cold nor hot. what is the letter's goal?
o: to wake you up, because you are loved.
games.why: the rebuke is fierce, but the letter says why: such as I love, I rebuke and chastise. and the next verse is a knock at the door.

practice: Pick one thing today you'd normally do half-there: the dishes, a walk, a talk with a child, a prayer, a piece of work.

Picture doing it with all of you, phone away, no rushing toward the next thing; not more effort, just more presence. If you pray, offer that one thing to God, done warmly; if not, simply commit to it in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Lukewarm. Apocalypse three: neither cold nor hot, neither refreshing nor healing, comfortable and half-there. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: lukewarm, tepid (Apocalypse 3:16), the only time the word appears in the New Testament.

carryVoice: Your line: not lukewarm. Hot heals, cold refreshes, and both are worth something. Until tomorrow.
